content: The pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data for clofazimine and bedaquiline in patients with complicated extrapulmonary tuberculosis (TB) are currently insufficient. As a result, it is not possible at this stage to recommend the use of the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) regimen for such patients. For patients with diabetes mellitus, there is no available data on the use of the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen in this population. While this regimen may be considered as a treatment option, it is advisable to closely monitor these patients for potential hepatotoxicity. Annex I outlines the dosages recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for both the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen and the longer all-oral regimens. Medications in these regimens are taken daily, seven days a week. Bedaquiline is administered daily for the first two weeks, followed by three times per week for the remaining 22 weeks. Further details on dosing and dose adjustments are provided in Annex I. In cases where treatment with the shorter MDR-TB regimen is interrupted for less than two months, the clinician must decide whether to continue the shorter regimen based on the patient’s clinical condition and repeat laboratory test results. The clinician must also determine whether the missed doses should be added to the remaining treatment or if a longer regimen should be initiated. Treatment response is monitored through monthly sputum smear microscopy and culture, ideally at the same frequency. This monitoring schedule is similar to that used for patients on longer all-oral MDR-TB regimens. The definitions of treatment outcomes and the reporting framework for patients on the shorter MDR-TB regimen are the same as those for patients on longer regimens. Although the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen is generally well-tolerated, the safety profile of some of the medications used concurrently may raise concerns. For example, the combination of clofazimine, bedaquiline, and high-dose moxifloxacin—all of which can prolong the QT interval—necessitates careful monitoring for additive cardiotoxicity using electrocardiograms (ECGs). Any adverse events experienced by patients on treatment must be reported to the national pharmacovigilance agency within the framework of an active drug safety monitoring and management (aDSM) system. A functional aDSM system must be in place before initiating patients on the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing MDR/RR-TB regimen. To ensure the collection of essential safety data for all patients starting treatment, preparations must be made for data collection in either paper or electronic format, and staff must be adequately trained to collect this data. All details of the patient’s diagnosis, drug susceptibility testing (DST), treatment, adverse effects, and outcomes must be recorded in accordance with good clinical practice. Routine monitoring or regular surveys should also be conducted to assess for emerging resistance to bedaquiline. National TB programs (NTPs) planning to pilot shorter MDR-TB regimens are advised to do so under operational research conditions. The Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR), in collaboration with the WHO Global TB Programme and technical partners, has developed the ShORRT (Short, all-Oral Regimens for Rifampicin-resistant Tuberculosis) operational research package. This package is designed to evaluate the effectiveness, safety, feasibility, acceptability, cost, and impact (including quality of life) of all-oral shorter drug regimens for patients with drug-resistant TB. All-oral shorter MDR-TB regimens typically consist of fouror five-drug standardized combinations. These regimens, currently being tested in randomized clinical trials, have been endorsed by scientific committees for testing. Their use under operational research conditions will contribute to the evidence base for these regimens. The ShORRT research package includes proposed modified regimens for testing under operational research conditions. When selecting an all-oral shorter MDR-TB regimen, it is crucial to ensure that the program can follow patients for one year post-treatment to monitor for recurrent TB. Additionally, there must be documentation that the regimen does not result in a high relapse rate. Modified all-oral shorter MDR-TB regimens, which differ from the recommended bedaquiline-based shorter regimen, should only be implemented under operational research conditions. These conditions require a study protocol with a 12-month follow-up after treatment, a clinical treatment guide with a patient consent process, approval by the national ethics review board or ministry of health, and at least an aDSM core package. Longer MDR-TB regimens are available for all MDR/RR-TB patients but are preferably used for those who are not eligible for shorter all-oral regimens, including patients with quinolone resistance. In settings with limited access to reliable DST, NTPs often standardize longer regimens. However, individualized regimens may enhance effectiveness and safety in certain cases. Longer regimens should include all three Group A agents and at least one Group B agent to ensure that treatment starts with at least four effective TB agents. If only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents should be included. Group C agents may be added if necessary to complete the regimen. Certain drugs, such as kanamycin and capreomycin, should not be included in longer MDR-TB regimens. Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid should be included in these regimens. Clofazimine, cycloserine, or terizidone may also be included. Ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, imipenem-cilastatin, or meropenem may be used in specific circumstances. Amikacin may be included for patients aged 18 years or older if susceptibility is demonstrated and adequate monitoring for adverse reactions is ensured. If amikacin is unavailable, streptomycin may replace it under the same conditions. Ethionamide or prothionamide and p-aminosalicylic acid should only be included if better options are not available. Clavulanic acid should not be included in MDR/RR-TB regimens. All patients considered for longer MDR-TB regimens must have a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis of MDR/RR-TB before starting treatment with second-line medicines. This is necessary to avoid unnecessary exposure to lengthy and toxic treatment regimens that may be less effective than rifampicin-based regimens for drug-susceptible TB. Resistance to additional drugs may be present at baseline or uncovered during treatment. Reliable DST is essential to guide the composition of both shorter and longer regimens, particularly for resistance to fluoroquinolones and other second-line drugs.
